meanings: (old) person specialized in a skill or trade

example.hanzi: 她去年拿到了博士学位。
example.pinyin: Tā qùnián nádào le bóshì xuéwèi.
example.english: She got her doctorate last year.
example.fact: 博士 literally reads as "broadly learned scholar" — 博 ("extensive, broad", tied here to 十 "ten" as a symbol of completeness) plus 士 ("scholar, gentleman") — and this literal sense was mapped directly onto the modern Western academic title "PhD" when Chinese needed a term for it in the early 20th century.

components.note: 十 (ten) — 博 relates to breadth, with ten symbolizing completeness.
尃 (fū) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading bó has diverged considerably.

example.pinyin: Tā zhídào shēnyè cái huí jiā.
example.english: He didn't come home until late at night.
example.fact: 直到 commonly pairs with 才 in the pattern "直到 X, 才 Y" ("not until X did Y happen") — 才 carries the "only then" emphasis, so dropping it (直到深夜他回家了) sounds noticeably flatter to a native ear, one of several such fixed adverb pairings in Mandarin.

components.note: 十 (here a straight vertical line) — 直 pictures something drawn perfectly straight.
目 (eye) — looking directly and steadily with the eye gave 直 its meaning 'straight' or 'direct.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.pinyin: Kǎoshì qián wǒ hěn jǐnzhāng.
example.english: I'm very nervous before the exam.
example.fact: 紧 (from 糸, thread pulled taut) and 张 (from 弓, a bow drawn taut) each independently picture something pulled tight — 紧张 stacks two 'taut' images into one word, making its abstract sense 'tense, nervous' a remarkably direct metaphor: feeling strung as tight as a drawn bowstring.

components.note: 糸 (silk/thread) — 紧 relates to something pulled taut, as thread is pulled tight when spun, giving its meaning 'tight, tense'
弓 (bow) — relates to 张's original meaning 'to draw a bow taut,' extended to 'to open, stretch.'
长 (cháng) gives a sound hint — 张 is pronounced zhāng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant and tone differ.

example.pinyin: Zhège jiàgé jiǎnzhí tài guì le!
example.english: This price is simply outrageous!
example.fact: Despite its parts literally meaning something closer to "simple" (简, from bamboo writing strips) and "straight" (直), 简直 functions as a pure intensifying adverb meaning "simply, just" before an exaggerated claim — much like English "simply" in "that's simply amazing" has drifted away from its literal sense of ease.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 简 originally referred to bamboo strips used for writing
间 (jiān) gives a sound close to 简's reading jiǎn, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
十 (here a straight vertical line) — 直 pictures something drawn perfectly straight.
目 (eye) — looking directly and steadily with the eye gave 直 its meaning 'straight' or 'direct.'

example.pinyin: Bié fàngqì nǐ de mèngxiǎng.
example.english: Don't give up on your dream.
example.fact: 放 ("to release, let go") plus 弃 (pictured as two hands 廾 casting aside a bundled object) combine almost literally into "to let go and throw away" — one of the more transparent compositional images in this batch, directly mirroring its modern sense "to give up, abandon."

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.
亠厶-shaped top pictures a bundled object being cast away.
廾 (two hands) below shows the act of throwing it out, giving 弃 its meaning 'to abandon, discard.'

example.pinyin: Nàge xiǎozi pǎo de zhēn kuài.
example.english: That kid runs really fast.
example.fact: 小子 has two dictionary readings that are easy to conflate: the common, informal xiǎozi ("boy, lad, kid" — often a gruff or teasing address, as in 你这小子 "you little punk") that accounts for the word's real frequency, and a separate literary xiǎozǐ ("young man"; also an old, self-effacing "I/me" used when addressing an elder) — the same two characters, a different register entirely.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 晚饭后我们一起看电视。
example.pinyin: Wǎnfàn hòu wǒmen yìqǐ kàn diànshì.
example.english: After dinner we watch TV together.
example.fact: 电视 is a purely modern coinage — 电 ("electricity", itself a lightning-bolt pictograph reused for the modern concept) plus 视 ("to view") — following the same 电+X pattern behind 电话 ("electric speech" = telephone) and 电脑 ("electric brain" = computer), Mandarin's default strategy for naming 20th-century technology.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
见 (to see) — relates directly to 视's meaning 'to look at, view.'
礻 (a form of 示, shì) gives the sound — 视 is also pronounced shì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 不好意思,请问洗手间在哪儿?
example.pinyin: Bùhǎoyìsi, qǐngwèn xǐshǒujiān zài nǎr?
example.english: Excuse me, where is the restroom?
example.fact: 不好意思 works as a softer, more versatile cousin of 对不起: 对不起 apologizes for a real fault, while 不好意思 covers everything from mild embarrassment to a polite "(sorry to bother you,) excuse me" used to open a request to a stranger — a nuance its literal gloss, "not good meaning," doesn't capture at all.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
An altered form of 囟 (the mind/head) — the seat of thought.
心 (heart) — thinking was pictured as an activity of both mind and heart, giving 思 its meaning 'to think.'

example.hanzi: 我们大概需要两个小时。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dàgài xūyào liǎng gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: We probably need about two hours.
example.fact: 概 originally named a wooden bar used to level off excess grain when measuring by the bushel — striking a rough, standard level rather than an exact one. That image of 'close enough, roughly leveled' carried over almost directly into 大概's modern sense, 'roughly, approximately.'

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
木 (wood) — 概 originally referred to a wooden leveling bar used to strike excess grain off a measure, later extended to 'in general, roughly'
既 (jì) gives a sound distantly related to 概's reading gài, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Zhè díquè shì gè hǎo zhǔyi.
example.english: This really is a good idea.
example.fact: 的确 borrows the ubiquitous particle 的 (elsewhere just a possessive/adjective marker, as in 我的书 "my book") and fuses it with 确 ("true, certain") into a fixed adverb meaning "indeed, really" — a reminder that 的 shows up in several unrelated fixed words beyond its famous grammatical role.

components.note: 石 (stone) — 确 originally meant firm and solid like stone, extending to 'true, accurate, indeed.'
角 (jiǎo) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from què.

example.pinyin: Tā zhōngyú huídào le jiā.
example.english: He finally returned home.
example.fact: 到 here works as a resultative verb complement meaning "the goal was reached" rather than a separate verb "to arrive" — attaching directly after 回 ("to return") to confirm the destination was reached, the same complement pattern that turns 收 ("to gather") into 收到 ("to receive") elsewhere in this batch.

components.note: 回 depicts a spiral or winding shape — something that turns back on itself, giving rise to the meaning 'to return.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.pinyin: Nàge nánhái xǐhuan tī zúqiú.
example.english: That boy likes playing soccer.
example.fact: 男 pictures 力 ('strength') applied to 田 ('a field') — someone strong enough to farm, an agrarian image behind the character for 'male' — so 男孩 literally reads as 'strong-in-the-field child,' though today it's simply the everyday word for 'boy.'

components.note: 田 (field) — represents farmland.
力 (strength/effort) — someone strong enough to work the fields gave 男 its meaning 'male, man.'
子 (child) — 孩 relates directly to children
亥 (hài) gives a sound close to 孩's reading hái

example.pinyin: Wǒ hěn xǐhuan gǔdiǎn yīnyuè.
example.english: I really like classical music.
example.fact: 乐 is a genuine two-reading character: yuè for "music" (as here) and lè for "happy" (as in 快乐, "happy") — historically linked since music was seen as a source of joy, but a learner has to memorize which compound takes which reading, since guessing wrong (yīnlè instead of yīnyuè) is a common beginner slip.

components.note: 立 here depicts a tongue positioned to speak.
日 here depicts an open mouth — a tongue forming sound in the mouth gave 音 its meaning 'sound, tone.'
乐 is the simplified form of 樂, which depicted a wooden 木 instrument strung with strings 幺, played with a pick 白 — music came to represent joy, giving 乐 its meaning 'happy, music.'

example.pinyin: Nǐ shēntǐ hǎo ma?
example.english: How is your health?
example.fact: 身体 doubles as the everyday word for general health and physical condition beyond its literal sense "body" — asking 你身体好吗 ("is your body good?") is really asking "how is your health," a common greeting especially toward elders, not a question about physique.

components.note: 身 depicts a person's torso, originally showing a pregnant woman's body — later broadened to mean 'the body' in general.

example.pinyin: Tā bǎ yàoshi liúxià le.
example.english: He left the keys behind.
example.fact: 下 attached after a verb often marks something coming to rest or settling in place (坐下 'sit down', 停下 'stop') — 留下 uses that same complement to turn 留 ('to remain') into a precise 'leave behind, stay put', distinguishing it from 留 alone, which can also mean the more active 'to keep, retain' something.

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 每个人都有自己的学习方式。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén dōu yǒu zìjǐ de xuéxí fāngshì.
example.english: Everyone has their own way of learning.
example.fact: 式 pictures a craftsman's tools — 弋 (an awl) and 工 (a measuring square) — used to make things to a fixed pattern, which is why so many "-式" words name a fixed style or method (方式 "way, method"; 正式 "formal"; 公式 "formula").

components.note: 弋 (an awl or tool) — one of the craftsman's instruments.
工 (a measuring square) — a tool for making things to a fixed pattern, giving 式 its meaning 'style, form, type.'

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn wàitào yào yìbǎi měiyuán.
example.english: This jacket costs a hundred dollars.
example.fact: 元 (from an image emphasizing a person's head — "first, foremost") became Mandarin's generic word for a basic currency unit, filled in by the country name: 美元 ("American" + 元) for the US dollar, 日元 for the Japanese yen, 欧元 for the Euro — the same slot, a different country each time.

components.note: 羊 (sheep; here representing feathers or ornaments on a headdress) — an elaborate decoration worn on the head.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — a person wearing a decorated headdress was seen as beautiful, giving 美 its meaning 'beautiful.'
儿 (a standing person) — the figure being emphasized.
二 (an extra line at the top) — emphasizing the person's head, the 'first, foremost' part of them — the source of 元's meanings 'origin, first' and, by extension, the basic unit of Chinese currency.

example.hanzi: 他因为偷东西被送进了监狱。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi tōu dōngxi bèi sòngjìn le jiānyù.
example.english: He was sent to prison for stealing.
example.fact: 狱's own components stack two dog radicals (犭and 犬) around 讠("speech, dispute") — traditionally read as two dogs snarling on either side of an argument — a vivid ancient courtroom image behind the modern word for "prison, lawsuit."

components.note: 犭 (dog) on the left represents a guard dog.
讠 (speech) suggests an accusation or a legal case being spoken.
犬 (dog) on the right completes the scene, giving 狱 its meaning 'prison, lawsuit.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng wǎng zhèbiān zǒu.
example.english: Please come this way.
example.fact: 这边 pairs with 那边 ("that side") the same way 这个/那个 do — but where 这里 ("here") names a fixed point, 这边 leans toward a direction or side, which is why staff say 这边请 ("this way, please") rather than 这里请 when guiding someone somewhere.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — links 边's meaning to a boundary or edge one moves along.
臱 (biān) gives the sound — 边 is also pronounced biān, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Qǐng chóngxīn tiánxiě zhè zhāng biǎogé.
example.english: Please fill out this form again, from scratch.
example.fact: 重新 implies starting completely over from scratch (重新开始 "start over"), while its near-synonym 再 just means "once more" without necessarily redoing everything (再说一次 "say it again") — a distinction easy to blur since English "again" covers both.

components.note: 千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'
亲 (here representing a tree, related to 榛/hazel) — 新 pictures a tree being cut.
斤 (an axe) — freshly chopping wood gave 新 its meaning of something 'new' or 'fresh.'

example.hanzi: 演唱会现场的粉丝们疯狂地欢呼。
example.pinyin: Yǎnchànghuì xiànchǎng de fěnsīmen fēngkuáng de huānhū.
example.english: The fans at the concert cheered wildly.
example.fact: 狂 traces back to a rabid, mad dog (犭), while 疯 pairs the "sickness" radical 疒 with the phonetic 风 ("wind") — pairing an illness-word for madness with an animal-word for wildness, 疯狂 doubles up two independently vivid pictures of losing control.

components.note: 疒 (sickness) shows 疯 describes an afflicted state of mind.
风 (fēng) gives the exact sound of 疯.
犭 (dog) — 狂 originally described a mad, rabid dog, extending to 'wild, crazy.'
王 (wáng) gives a sound distantly related to kuáng, having drifted apart over time.

example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān shōudào le nǐ de xìn.
example.english: I received your letter yesterday.
example.fact: 收 alone just means 'to gather, collect' without guaranteeing success — attaching the complement 到 ('arriving, reaching') turns it into 收到, confirming that whatever was sent actually arrived, the same success-marking job 到 does after 看 (看到, 'to see') and 听 (听到, 'to hear').

components.note: 攵 (a hand with an implement) — relates to 收's meaning 'to receive, collect, harvest.'
丩 (jiū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shōu.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我们讨论了几个方案,其中一个很有创意。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen tǎolùn le jǐ gè fāng'àn, qízhōng yí gè hěn yǒu chuàngyì.
example.english: We discussed a few proposals, one of which was very creative.
example.fact: 其中 always points back to a group already named in the sentence or context — it can't introduce a brand-new set the way English "among" sometimes can, which is why it almost always follows a list or plural noun ("几个方案,其中...") rather than opening a sentence on its own.

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 我对这个问题有不同的想法。
example.pinyin: Wǒ duì zhège wèntí yǒu bùtóng de xiǎngfǎ.
example.english: I have a different idea about this issue.
example.fact: 法 pictures water (氵) following a fixed course (去) — a natural, regulated way of flowing that gave the character its sense "method, way" — 想法 literally combines this with 想 ("to think") into "a way of thinking," Mandarin's everyday word for a personal idea or opinion.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 想 relates to thinking, missing someone, or wanting something in one's heart.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — 想 is pronounced xiǎng, matching aside from tone.
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.hanzi: 我下个月要去纽约旅行。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xiàgèyuè yào qù Niǔyuē lǚxíng.
example.english: I'm traveling to New York next month.
example.fact: 纽约 is a pure sound-transliteration of "New York" — 纽 ("knot, button") and 约 ("approximately, to agree") were picked only for how close niǔ-yuē sounds to the English name, with no attempt to translate the actual meaning of "new" or "york," unlike semantic coinages such as 电视 ("electric-view" for television) elsewhere in this batch.

components.note: Thread/silk — early buttons and knots were tied with thread.
Gives the sound chǒu, related to niǔ but drifted apart over time.
纟 (thread) — 约 originally meant 'to bind, tie up,' extending to 'to agree, arrange' and 'approximately.'

example.pinyin: Māma zài jiālǐ zuòfàn.
example.english: Mom is cooking at home.
example.fact: 家 alone can mean "home" as an abstract concept or "family," but 家里 anchors it with 里 ("inside") to mean specifically "inside the house, at home" as a physical location — the difference shows up in phrases like 回家 ("go home," a destination) versus 在家里 ("be at home," a location).

components.note: 宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.pinyin: Wǒ háiyào yì bēi kāfēi, xièxie.
example.english: I'd like one more cup of coffee, thanks.
example.fact: 还要 stacks two separate senses of 还 — "still" (as in 还没, "not yet") and "in addition, also" — onto 要 ("to want, need, will"), so depending on context it can mean "I still want (more)" (我还要一个) or "I also need to (do something)" (我还要去银行), two related but distinct translations packed into the same two characters.

components.note: 辶 (to walk/move) — relates to motion or progress.
不 (not) — 'not yet moving on' gave 还 its meaning of 'still, yet.'
女 (woman) with 覀 depicting hands on the waist — an old image of insisting or demanding something, connected to 要's meaning 'to want, to need.'

example.pinyin: Yínháng jiù zài chāoshì hòumian.
example.english: The bank is right behind the supermarket.
example.fact: 面 (originally a pictograph of a face) works as a locative suffix turning a direction into a place-noun — 后面 ("behind") mirrors 前面 ("in front"), 上面 ("above"), and 里面 ("inside"), all built from the same "-面" pattern for naming relative position.

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 这个消息给大家带来了希望。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiāoxi gěi dàjiā dàilái le xīwàng.
example.english: This news brought hope to everyone.
example.fact: 带 ("to carry along") plus the directional complement 来 ("toward the speaker") literally means "carry here" — but 带来 is used just as often in its figurative sense, "to bring about (a result, an effect)," as in 带来影响 ("to bring about an impact"), extending the physical carrying image to abstract causes and consequences.

components.note: 巾 (cloth) — the bottom half of a belt, hanging straight down.
Above the cloth, the strokes crease as if folded at the waist — depicting a belt or sash, the source of 带's meaning 'belt, band,' later 'to bring, carry along.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.pinyin: Zuótiān wǎnshang xiàyǔ le.
example.english: It rained last night.
example.fact: 昨 never appears alone as a stand-alone word in modern Mandarin — it only shows up bound to a time word, as in 昨天 ('yesterday') or the more literary 昨夜 ('last night'), unlike its partner 天, which functions perfectly well by itself to mean 'day' or 'sky.'

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — 昨 relates to a day, specifically the one before today.
乍 (zhà) is only distantly related in sound to zuó — the connection has drifted apart over time.
大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'

example.pinyin: Zhèyàng zuò bù hǎo.
example.english: It's not good to do it this way.
example.fact: 不好 attached right after certain verbs takes on the idiomatic sense "hard to, difficult to" beyond plainly negating 好 ("good") — 不好说 doesn't mean "bad to say" but "hard to say," and 不好办 means a matter is "difficult to handle," a shift a literal word-by-word reading misses.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
女 (woman) — represents a mother.
子 (child/son) — a mother together with her child was seen as an image of goodness, giving 好 its meaning 'good.'

example.pinyin: Tā yíxiàzi zhuāzhù le jīhuì.
example.english: He seized the opportunity in an instant.
example.fact: 住 as a verb complement marks something being secured or held fast, not just touched briefly — the same 住 turns 记 ("to note, remember") into 记住 ("commit to memory"), and 站 ("to stand") into 站住 ("stand firm, stop right there"), a small but recurring complement family built around the idea of "staying put."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抓 describes an action done by hand, grabbing.
爪 depicts claws or fingers gripping something, reinforcing 抓's meaning 'to grab, to seize.'
亻 (person) — the one settling somewhere.
主 (host, master) — the idea of a person settled in a place as if hosting it, giving 住 its meaning 'to live, reside, stay.'

example.hanzi: 请把会议内容记录下来。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ huìyì nèiróng jìlù xiàlai.
example.english: Please record the content of the meeting.
example.fact: 记录 pairs two independently "recording"-flavored characters: 记 (built from 讠 "speech" plus 己 "oneself," originally writing down one's own notes) and 录 (a pictograph of a hand tool used for carving records) — like 紧张 elsewhere in this very batch, another case of Mandarin reinforcing a meaning by doubling near-synonymous halves.

components.note: 讠 (speech/writing) — the act of putting words down.
己 (oneself, private) — writing down one's own private notes or memories, giving 记 its meaning 'to record, remember.'
录 traditionally depicted a hand-held tool used for carving or writing records — the image behind its meaning 'to record, to write down.'

example.pinyin: Qǐng zài gěi wǒ yìdiǎnr shíjiān.
example.english: Please give me a little more time.
example.fact: The 儿 in 点儿 isn't the word for 'child' — it's 'erhua,' a suffix that fuses onto a syllable as a retroflex -r sound, common in Beijing-flavored Mandarin to add a light, casual, often diminutive flavor. 点儿 and plain 点 are largely interchangeable, but the erhua form reads as noticeably more colloquial.

components.note: 灬 (fire) — 点 originally related to a small flame or dot of light, giving rise to the meaning 'dot' or 'point.'
占 (zhàn) gives a hint of the sound — 点 is pronounced diǎn, a connection that has drifted over the centuries.
儿 (simplified from 兒) depicts a small child, drawn with a large head on a small body — a simple picture of youth.

meanings: (form of address between male friends) old chap

example.pinyin: Lǎoxiōng, hǎojiǔ bújiàn!
example.english: Buddy, long time no see!
example.fact: The 老 in 老兄 doesn't mean the person is actually old — as a prefix before a term of address (老兄, 老张, 老朋友) 老 signals familiarity and warmth rather than age, the same affectionate "老 + name/role" pattern Chinese uses for close friends of any age.

components.note: 耂 (a person bent with age, with long hair) — depicts an elderly figure.
匕 (here representing a cane or walking stick) — combined with the bent figure above, 老 pictures an old person leaning on a cane.
口 (mouth) pictures someone speaking.
儿 (person) below gives the shape of a person, together showing an elder brother speaking to his siblings.

example.hanzi: 这些学生来自不同的国家。
example.pinyin: Zhèxiē xuésheng láizì bùtóng de guójiā.
example.english: These students come from different countries.
example.fact: 来自 sits at a more formal, written register than the everyday spoken pattern 从...来 ("come from...") — it shows up constantly in bios, news reports, and official introductions (来自中国的代表, "a representative from China"), but would sound slightly stiff in casual conversation, where 从哪儿来 is more natural.

components.note: Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'
A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'

example.hanzi: 我妹妹明年要上大学了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ mèimei míngnián yào shàng dàxué le.
example.english: My younger sister is going to start university next year.
example.fact: 学 (a roof 冖 sheltering 子 "child") shows up scaled by size rather than by grade or age band the way English does: 小学 ("small learning") is elementary school, 中学 ("middle learning") is secondary school, and 大学 ("great learning") is university — a size metaphor for increasing scope of study.

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.

example.hanzi: 她每天都要照顾生病的爸爸。
example.pinyin: Tā měitiān dōu yào zhàogu shēngbìng de bàba.
example.english: She has to take care of her sick father every day.
example.fact: 照 ("to shine light on, illuminate") and 顾 ("to turn one's head and look back at") combine into a caring, watchful gaze — 照顾 pictures someone keeping an attentive eye on another person, a fittingly gentle literal image behind the everyday word for "to take care of."

components.note: 灬 (fire) — relates to 照's meaning 'to shine, illuminate; photograph.'
昭 (zhāo) gives a sound hint — 照 is pronounced zhào, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.
页 (head) — 顾 originally related to turning the head to look back at something
厄 (è) gives a sound distantly related to 顾's reading gù, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Wáng tàitai, hǎojiǔ bújiàn!
example.english: Mrs. Wang, long time no see!
example.fact: 太太 sits at the polite, formal end of a spectrum of words for "wife": 妻子 is the neutral, written-register term, 老婆 is the casual, affectionate one, and 太太 (also doubling as the polite title "Mrs.") is what you'd use to address or refer respectfully to someone else's wife, like 王太太 for "Mrs. Wang."

components.note: 太 adds a small dot below 大 (big) — the extra mark emphasizes something even bigger or more extreme, giving 太 its meaning 'too' or 'extremely.'
太 adds a small dot below 大 (big) — the extra mark emphasizes something even bigger or more extreme, giving 太 its meaning 'too' or 'extremely.'

example.pinyin: Zhè zhī gǒu fēicháng cōngming.
example.english: This dog is very clever.
example.fact: 聪 traces back to 耳 ("ear"), since sharp hearing was seen as a marker of mental acuity, while 明 pictures the combined brightness of 日 ("sun") and 月 ("moon") — 聪明 literally reads as "sharp of ear, bright as sun-and-moon," pairing acute perception with brilliance into the everyday word for "smart, clever."

components.note: 耳 (ear) shows 聪 relates to hearing, extended to mean sharp intelligence.
总 (zǒng) gives a sound close to cōng, sharing a similar consonant sound.
日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.

example.hanzi: 我本来想去旅行,但是没有时间。
example.pinyin: Wǒ běnlái xiǎng qù lǚxíng, dànshì méiyǒu shíjiān.
example.english: I originally wanted to travel, but I didn't have time.
example.fact: 本来 almost always sets up an implicit contrast with what actually happened — "originally/at first X, but then Y" — even when 但是 or 结果 isn't spoken aloud, a listener expects the sentence to pivot away from the original plan, similar to how English "originally" implies a plan that changed.

components.note: 木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 大家一起为运动员加油!
example.pinyin: Dàjiā yìqǐ wèi yùndòngyuán jiāyóu!
example.english: Everyone cheer for the athletes together!
example.fact: 加油 literally means "to add oil/fuel" (as at a gas station) but has become one of Mandarin's most common cheering exclamations — shouted alone as 加油! ("go for it! you've got this!") at sports events, exams, and any moment someone needs encouragement, extending the fueling image to a boost of effort.

components.note: 力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'
氵 (water) — 油 names an oily liquid.
由 (yóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 油.

example.hanzi: 实际上,这个计划根本不可行。
example.pinyin: Shíjìshàng, zhège jìhuà gēnběn bù kěxíng.
example.english: In fact, this plan isn't feasible at all.
example.fact: 上 here works as an abstract locative suffix meaning roughly "on the level/plane of" rather than physical "on top of" — the same pattern shows up in 基本上 ("basically," literally "on the basic level") and 理论上 ("theoretically," "on the theoretical level"), a recurring way Mandarin turns a noun into "from the X standpoint."

components.note: 阝 (a mound/place) — relates to 际's meaning 'border, between,' an edge or boundary marker.
示 (shì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jì.
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.pinyin: Nǐ zài zhèlǐ zhù le duōjiǔ?
example.english: How long have you lived here?
example.fact: 多久 belongs to a whole family of "多 + adjective" questions asking for a measurement — 多大 ("how old/big"), 多高 ("how tall"), 多久 ("how long, of time") — the same productive pattern that lets 多 turn almost any scalar adjective into its corresponding question word.

components.note: 夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.hanzi: 他工作努力,并且十分负责。
example.pinyin: Tā gōngzuò nǔlì, bìngqiě shífēn fùzé.
example.english: He works hard and is also very responsible.
example.fact: 并且 sits at a more formal, written register than its everyday synonym 而且 — both mean "moreover, and," but 并且 shows up far more in reports, contracts, and formal writing, while 而且 dominates ordinary conversation, a register distinction the English gloss doesn't capture.

components.note: 并 (simplified from 並) depicts two people standing side by side — giving its meaning of 'together' or 'and.'
Originally a pictograph of a stone altar or ancestral tablet; its later use as the grammatical word 且, 'moreover, and,' has no connection to that original picture.

meanings: direct (opposite: indirect 間接|间接[jian4 jie1])

example.pinyin: Nǐ kěyǐ zhíjiē liánxì wǒ.
example.english: You can contact me directly.
example.fact: 直 ("straight," pictured as an eye 目 looking fixedly ahead) plus 接 ("to connect") combine transparently into "a straight connection" — giving 直接 its modern sense "direct, immediate," whether describing a flight with no layovers or a blunt, straightforward way of speaking.

components.note: 十 (here a straight vertical line) — 直 pictures something drawn perfectly straight.
目 (eye) — looking directly and steadily with the eye gave 直 its meaning 'straight' or 'direct.'
扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 对于这个问题,大家意见不一。
example.pinyin: Duìyú zhège wèntí, dàjiā yìjiàn bùyī.
example.english: Regarding this issue, people have different opinions.
example.fact: 对于 and its near-synonym 关于 both translate as "about, regarding," but they lean differently: 对于 usually introduces something people react to or take a stance on, while 关于 more neutrally names a topic of discussion (关于这个问题的报告, "a report about this issue") — a nuance easy to miss when both get flattened to "about" in English.

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.pinyin: Tiānqì tūrán biànlěng le.
example.english: The weather suddenly turned cold.
example.fact: 突 pictures a dog (犬) bursting suddenly out of its den (穴) — a vivid, almost cinematic image of something unexpected breaking loose — which 突然 then generalizes into the everyday adverb for anything happening "suddenly, abruptly."

components.note: 穴 (a cave/hole) — the den the dog bursts from.
犬 (dog) — a dog suddenly darting out of its den gave 突 its meaning 'sudden, abrupt.'
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Jǐngchá duìzhe lúntāi kāiqiāng le.
example.english: The police fired at the tire.
example.fact: 开 here means neither "to open" nor even its more familiar "to start/operate" sense in isolation — 开枪 belongs to a wide family of 开 + noun collocations for activating something (开车 "to drive," literally "operate a car"; 开灯 "to turn on a light," literally "open a light"), with "firing a gun" folded into the same pattern as flipping a switch.

components.note: 廾 (two hands) — depicts hands at work.
一 represents the latch or bar of a door; hands lifting it away gave 开 its meaning 'to open, to start.'
木 (wood) — early spears and rifle stocks were made of wood.
仓 (cāng) gives a sound close to qiāng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 除非你道歉,否则我不会原谅你。
example.pinyin: Chúfēi nǐ dàoqiàn, fǒuzé wǒ bú huì yuánliàng nǐ.
example.english: Unless you apologize, I won't forgive you.
example.fact: 除非 commonly pairs with 否则 or 不然 ("otherwise") in the fixed frame "除非 X, 否则 Y" ("unless X, otherwise Y") — the same paired-conjunction habit behind 因为...所以... elsewhere in this deck, where Mandarin keeps both halves of a logical relationship spoken explicitly rather than dropping one as redundant.

components.note: 阝 (a mound/settlement) — represents a city or town.
余 (surplus, remainder) — the leftover waste a city produces, which must be cleared away, giving 除 its meaning 'to remove, eliminate.'
Depicts two things splayed apart from each other — such as a bird's two wings, or two people standing back-to-back — later used for the meaning 'not, contrary to.'
